mechanism: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal perfusion, worsening GFR and causing fluid/sodium retention and hyperkalaemia.
recommendation: Avoid in moderate-to-severe CKD; if unavoidable use the lowest dose briefly with renal monitoring.

mechanism: Sodium and fluid retention plus reduced renal perfusion can precipitate decompensation and blunt diuretic effect.
recommendation: Avoid NSAIDs in heart failure; use paracetamol for analgesia.

mechanism: COX-1 inhibition impairs gastroprotective prostaglandins, increasing ulceration and GI bleeding risk.
recommendation: Avoid in active or prior peptic ulcer disease; if essential, co-prescribe a proton-pump inhibitor.

mechanism: Reduced renal clearance causes metformin accumulation, raising the risk of lactic acidosis.
recommendation: Withhold metformin in AKI and in severe CKD (eGFR <30); reassess before restarting.

mechanism: Tissue hypoperfusion/hypoxia in acute decompensation increases lactic acidosis risk.
recommendation: Avoid during acute decompensation/hypoxia; stable chronic heart failure with preserved renal function is not a contraindication.

mechanism: Beta-2 blockade can precipitate severe bronchospasm.
recommendation: Avoid non-selective beta-blockers in asthma; a cardioselective agent may be used cautiously when strongly indicated.

mechanism: Foetotoxic in the 2nd/3rd trimester — oligohydramnios, renal dysgenesis, skull defects.
recommendation: Stop ACE inhibitors/ARBs before or as soon as pregnancy is confirmed; switch to a pregnancy-safe antihypertensive (e.g. labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine).

mechanism: Reduced aldosterone lowers potassium excretion, worsening hyperkalaemia.
recommendation: Avoid starting in significant hyperkalaemia; monitor potassium and renal function after initiation/dose change.

mechanism: Aldosterone antagonism reduces potassium excretion, risking dangerous hyperkalaemia, especially with CKD or RAAS inhibitors.
recommendation: Avoid in significant hyperkalaemia or severe renal impairment; monitor potassium closely.

mechanism: Inadequate urinary concentration when eGFR is low reduces efficacy and increases systemic toxicity.
recommendation: Avoid if eGFR <45 mL/min (short-course use with caution at 30–44 may be considered per local guidance).

mechanism: Oxidant stress can precipitate acute haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients.
recommendation: Avoid in known G6PD deficiency; choose an alternative urinary antimicrobial.

mechanism: Causes fluid retention that can precipitate or worsen heart failure.
recommendation: Do not use in heart failure or a history of heart failure.

mechanism: 5-HT1B-mediated vasoconstriction can provoke coronary spasm and ischaemia.
recommendation: Avoid triptans in established ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension or prior MI.

mechanism: Central D2 antagonism worsens parkinsonian motor symptoms and antagonises dopaminergic therapy.
recommendation: Avoid in Parkinson disease; use domperidone (peripheral D2 antagonist) or ondansetron for nausea.

mechanism: Associated with increased risk of stroke and all-cause mortality in older people with dementia.
recommendation: Avoid routine use; reserve for severe distress/risk at the lowest dose for the shortest time after non-drug measures.

condition: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
mechanism: Negative inotropy can worsen systolic heart failure.
recommendation: Avoid verapamil/diltiazem in HFrEF; use a heart-failure-indicated beta-blocker for rate control.

mechanism: Oestrogen further raises the already-increased ischaemic stroke risk in migraine with aura.
recommendation: Avoid combined hormonal contraception; offer progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods.

references.label: UK/WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

mechanism: Oestrogen increases venous thromboembolism risk.
recommendation: Avoid in current or prior VTE; use progestogen-only or non-hormonal contraception.

mechanism: Potential hepatotoxicity; transaminases may rise.
recommendation: Avoid starting in active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevation >3x ULN; recheck LFTs.

mechanism: Starting urate-lowering therapy during a flare can prolong or worsen it by mobilising urate.
recommendation: Do not start allopurinol during an acute flare; begin once settled, under anti-inflammatory cover. If already established, continue through the flare.

mechanism: Unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
recommendation: Never give a beta-blocker before adequate alpha-blockade in phaeochromocytoma.

mechanism: Further suppression of AV conduction and heart rate can cause haemodynamic collapse.
recommendation: Avoid in second/third-degree AV block (without pacemaker) or symptomatic bradycardia.

mechanism: Immunosuppression can worsen or mask infection (including reactivation of TB or strongyloidiasis).
recommendation: Use with caution; treat/exclude serious infection, screen for latent TB/strongyloides before prolonged high-dose therapy.

mechanism: Further QT prolongation increases the risk of torsades de pointes.
recommendation: Avoid in congenital/acquired long QT; correct electrolytes and review concomitant QT-prolonging drugs.

mechanism: COX-1 inhibition impairs gastric mucosal defence (prostaglandin-mediated mucus and bicarbonate secretion) and adds an antiplatelet bleeding effect; precipitates ulcer recurrence and bleeding.
recommendation: Avoid aspirin in active or recent peptic ulcer disease. If antiplatelet therapy is required for vascular indication, eradicate H. pylori, use a PPI, and consider clopidogrel only after specialist review.

references.label: ACG Guideline — peptic ulcer disease; BNF

condition: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter triad) / known NSAID-sensitive asthma
mechanism: COX-1 inhibition shifts arachidonic acid metabolism toward cysteinyl leukotrienes, precipitating bronchospasm in susceptible asthmatics (especially with nasal polyposis).
recommendation: Avoid aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs. Use paracetamol; if NSAID essential, consider a selective COX-2 inhibitor under specialist guidance with desensitisation if vascular indication.

references.label: GINA Asthma guidance; EAACI position paper on AERD

drug: Macrolide antibiotics (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin to a lesser degree)
mechanism: hERG (Ikr) potassium channel blockade prolongs cardiac repolarisation; risk of torsades de pointes amplified by congenital LQTS, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia or other QT-prolonging agents.
recommendation: Avoid macrolides (especially erythromycin and clarithromycin). Choose a non-QT-prolonging alternative (doxycycline, amoxicillin, β-lactam per indication).

references.label: CredibleMeds QT drug list; ESC LQTS management

mechanism: Oxidative stress can precipitate acute haemolysis in G6PD-deficient red cells, particularly during infection.
recommendation: Use with caution; prefer a non-oxidant antibiotic where appropriate. If used, monitor haemoglobin and haptoglobin and advise patient to seek care for jaundice, dark urine or pallor.

references.label: WHO Guide to G6PD deficiency in drug prescribing

mechanism: Strong oxidants — predictable haemolysis in G6PD-deficient erythrocytes, sometimes severe enough to require transfusion.
recommendation: Avoid in G6PD deficiency. Choose a non-oxidant alternative (e.g. pentamidine or atovaquone for PCP; macrolide or β-lactam for UTI per local susceptibility).

condition: Insulin-treated diabetes with hypoglycaemia awareness reliance
mechanism: Blunts adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia (tremor, tachycardia, palpitations) and inhibits gluconeogenesis; prolongs and masks hypoglycaemia.
recommendation: Prefer cardioselective β1-blockers (bisoprolol, metoprolol) at the lowest effective dose in insulin-treated diabetes; counsel patient about altered symptoms.

condition: Epilepsy / lowered seizure threshold (eating disorders, alcohol withdrawal)
mechanism: Dose-dependent reduction in seizure threshold (incidence 0.1–0.4% at therapeutic doses, much higher above maximum recommended dose).
recommendation: Do NOT prescribe in seizure disorders, current/past anorexia or bulimia, or during alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal. Choose an alternative antidepressant or smoking-cessation aid.

references.label: FDA label for bupropion; NICE depression guideline

condition: Chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 60 mL/min) or AKI
mechanism: Renally excreted with narrow therapeutic index; reduced clearance precipitates lithium toxicity. Long-term lithium itself can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and progressive CKD.
recommendation: Avoid initiating in significant CKD; if already established, reduce dose and monitor lithium level + U&E every 1–3 months. Hold during AKI or dehydration.

condition: Pregnancy / women of childbearing potential without effective contraception
mechanism: Major teratogen — neural tube defects (1–2%), cardiac and craniofacial malformations, plus long-term neurodevelopmental disability (autism, lower IQ) in up to 30–40% of exposed children.
recommendation: Do NOT prescribe to women of childbearing potential unless no alternative AND a pregnancy-prevention programme is in place (MHRA Valproate PPP). Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam when planning pregnancy.

references.label: MHRA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme (2018); WHO Essential Medicines warnings

mechanism: Lithium use in the first trimester is associated with cardiac malformations (Ebstein anomaly) — historically estimated ~1:1000 absolute risk above baseline; later trimesters risk neonatal toxicity and floppy-baby.
recommendation: Avoid where possible in the first trimester. If essential for severe bipolar disorder, use the lowest effective dose, monitor levels closely, perform fetal echocardiography at 16–20 weeks, plan delivery with neonatal/maternal teams.

references.label: NICE Bipolar disorder in pregnancy guideline; BNF

mechanism: Modest teratogenicity — neural tube defects (~1%), craniofacial and cardiac malformations; vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency in the neonate.
recommendation: Prefer lamotrigine or levetiracetam in women of childbearing potential. If carbamazepine remains essential, give high-dose folate (5 mg/day) pre-conception, monitor closely, and give vitamin K 10 mg PO to mother in the last month + 1 mg IM to neonate at birth.

references.label: NICE Epilepsy in pregnancy; UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register

mechanism: Major teratogen and abortifacient — folate antagonism causes craniofacial, limb and CNS malformations (methotrexate embryopathy).
recommendation: Absolute contraindication. Stop at least 3 months before attempting conception (longer per some guidance) in both women and men. Use effective contraception during therapy. Therapeutic use in pregnancy is restricted to ectopic pregnancy and termination protocols.

references.label: EULAR points to consider for prescribing in pregnancy (2016); FDA label

mechanism: Renal elimination is the dominant clearance route; reduced clearance produces myelosuppression, mucositis and hepatotoxicity, and impairs subsequent folinic acid rescue if needed.
recommendation: Avoid methotrexate in eGFR < 30. In eGFR 30–60 use reduced dose, monitor FBC and LFT weekly initially, ensure folate 5 mg weekly (taken on a different day).

mechanism: Statins block cholesterol biosynthesis required for fetal development (steroidogenesis, neural tissue); animal teratogenicity, limited human safety data.
recommendation: Discontinue at least 1 month before conception or as soon as pregnancy is confirmed; avoid during breastfeeding. Focus on lifestyle until delivery and end of breastfeeding, then resume.

references.label: FDA pregnancy labelling; NICE familial hypercholesterolaemia guideline

mechanism: Tetracyclines chelate calcium in developing teeth and bone, causing permanent tooth discolouration and (less commonly) transient bone-growth depression with prolonged courses.
recommendation: Avoid prolonged courses in children < 8 years and in pregnancy after the first trimester. Short courses (≤21 days) of doxycycline are now considered acceptable in younger children for life-threatening rickettsial disease and severe respiratory infection per CDC (2018 update).

references.label: CDC Yellow Book; AAP Red Book

mechanism: Cartilage and tendon toxicity in juvenile animal models; rare tendinitis / tendon rupture in humans (Achilles tendon, especially with corticosteroid co-treatment).
recommendation: Reserve for serious infections (complicated UTI / pyelonephritis, multidrug-resistant TB second-line, pseudomonas-coverage in cystic fibrosis) when no safer alternative exists. Counsel about tendon symptoms and avoid concomitant systemic steroids.

references.label: FDA fluoroquinolone safety communications; AAP Red Book

condition: Children under 12 years (and 12–18 years post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy or with OSA / obesity)
mechanism: Codeine is bioactivated to morphine by CYP2D6. Ultra-rapid metabolisers (1–7% of European, up to 30% of North African ancestry) produce excess morphine, with reports of fatal respiratory depression in children.
recommendation: Do NOT use codeine or tramadol in children <12 years for any indication, and in any child after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy. Choose paracetamol/ibuprofen first, then weight-appropriate morphine if needed.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication (2017); EMA recommendation (2013); WHO Pain Ladder review

mechanism: Maternal CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolism can yield high morphine concentrations in breast milk; reports of neonatal apnoea and death.
recommendation: Avoid codeine and tramadol while breastfeeding. Use paracetamol ± ibuprofen; if opioid required, low-dose morphine or fentanyl is preferred and the infant should be observed for sedation.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication (2017); UK Specialist Pharmacy Service

mechanism: Prostaglandin inhibition causes oligohydramnios, premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and fetal renal impairment after 20 weeks. Risk increases after 30 weeks.
recommendation: Avoid NSAIDs after 20 weeks. Use paracetamol; if anti-inflammatory required (severe inflammatory arthritis), specialist-supervised low-dose short course only.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication (2020); NICE Antenatal Care

mechanism: Renal elimination of unchanged bisphosphonate; IV zoledronate in renal impairment is associated with acute tubular necrosis. Oral bisphosphonates lack efficacy and safety data in advanced CKD.
recommendation: Avoid bisphosphonates when eGFR < 30–35 mL/min. Treat CKD-MBD per KDIGO; in CKD G4–5 use denosumab with vigilant calcium monitoring or refer to nephrology / metabolic bone.

references.label: KDIGO CKD-MBD guideline; FDA prescribing information for zoledronate

drug: Anticholinergic / antimuscarinic agents (oxybutynin, tolterodine, amitriptyline, first-generation antihistamines)
condition: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with bladder outflow obstruction
mechanism: Blockade of bladder detrusor muscarinic (M3) receptors reduces contractility; in significant outflow obstruction this precipitates acute urinary retention.
recommendation: Avoid where bladder outflow obstruction is suspected (high IPSS, large residual volume). If overactive bladder symptoms must be treated, consider mirabegron (β3-agonist) or refer urology.

references.label: BNF; EAU Non-neurogenic Male LUTS guideline

drug: Anticholinergic / antimuscarinic agents, tricyclic antidepressants, certain antiemetics (cyclizine), first-generation antihistamines
mechanism: Pupillary dilatation crowds the iridocorneal angle in eyes with anatomically narrow angles, precipitating acute angle-closure with rapid intraocular pressure rise and visual loss.
recommendation: Avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma. Open-angle glaucoma is not a contraindication.

references.label: BNF cautions; American Academy of Ophthalmology Primary Angle Closure PPP

condition: Uncontrolled hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, severe coronary artery disease
mechanism: α-adrenergic vasoconstriction raises blood pressure and afterload; reported myocardial infarction and hypertensive crisis in susceptible patients.
recommendation: Avoid systemic decongestants; advise saline nasal irrigation, topical decongestant (≤3 days) or intranasal steroid. Counsel patients on warfarin / MAOI about specific interactions.

condition: Children < 1 year (all uses) and routine use in young adults (extrapyramidal risk)
mechanism: Dopamine D2 blockade crosses the immature BBB readily, increasing the risk of acute dystonic reactions and tardive dyskinesia, particularly with prolonged or repeated use.
recommendation: Do NOT use in children < 1 year. In children 1–18 years and young adults, limit to short courses (≤5 days), use 0.1–0.15 mg/kg/dose to a maximum of 30 mg/day, and only for nausea/vomiting refractory to first-line treatment.

references.label: EMA review of metoclopramide (2013); BNF for Children

condition: Ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, sepsis
mechanism: Potent vasoconstriction (α-adrenergic and 5-HT1) can precipitate coronary or peripheral vascular ischaemia; ergotism with prolonged or co-administered CYP3A4 inhibitor use.
recommendation: Avoid in ischaemic / vascular disease. For migraine, prefer triptans (with their own cardiovascular cautions) or non-vasoconstrictive options (gepants where available, paracetamol/NSAID). For postpartum haemorrhage, use oxytocin first-line; reserve methylergometrine where appropriate, monitoring BP.

references.label: BNF; ACOG Postpartum Haemorrhage; WHO recommendations on prevention and treatment of PPH
